reviews.title: Real numbers and completeness · Chapter review

questions.problem: For nonempty bounded-above sets with $s=\sup A$ and $t=\sup B$, prove $\sup(A+B)=s+t$.
questions.hint: First give an upper bound, then approximate it from each set.
solution: Every sum is at most $s+t$.
For a positive error choose $a>s-\varepsilon/2,b>t-\varepsilon/2$.
Then $a+b>s+t-\varepsilon$.

questions.problem: Why does density of the rationals not imply their completeness?
questions.hint: Compare local approximation with membership of suprema.
solution: Rationals approximate the square root of two arbitrarily closely.
Their limit is irrational, and a supremum may lie outside the number system.

questions.problem: Prove a convergent real sequence has only one limit.
questions.hint: Divide the distance between proposed limits into thirds.
solution: If two distinct limits are distance $d>0$ apart, take error $d/3$.
Enter both tails and use the triangle inequality to make their distance less than two thirds of itself, a contradiction.

questions.problem: Give a bounded nonconvergent real sequence and identify two convergent subsequences.
solution: Odd and even subsequences tend to negative one and one respectively.
questions.answer: Boundedness guarantees a convergent subsequence only.

questions.problem: Prove convergence of $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/[n(n+1)]$ and find its sum.
questions.hint: Split into differences of adjacent reciprocals.
solution: Partial sums satisfy $1-1/(N+1)\to1$.

questions.problem: Can ratio limit one decide convergence? Give contrasting examples.
solution: The harmonic series diverges; reciprocal squares converge.
Both have ratio limit one.

reviews.title: Sets on the real line · Chapter review

questions.problem: For the reciprocal set together with zero, determine openness, closedness, boundedness, compactness, and connectedness.
questions.hint: Identify every limit point, then check for gaps.
solution: It is closed and bounded, hence compact.
It is not open; it skips intermediate points between separated members, so is disconnected.
questions.answer: Closed, bounded, compact; not open or connected.

questions.problem: Why can finite cover diagrams not directly verify compactness?
questions.hint: The definition quantifies over every open cover.
solution: A diagram checks only one cover.
A general finite-subcover argument or the proved Heine–Borel criterion is needed.
questions.answer: Finite examples do not replace a universal proof.

reviews.title: Continuity and uniform continuity · Chapter review

questions.problem: Prove squaring uniformly continuous on each fixed closed bounded interval, and explain why the full real line differs.
solution: On $[-M,M]$, $|x^2-y^2|\le2M|x-y|$; the case $M=0$ is trivial.
On the whole line choose $n,n+1/n$: input gaps vanish while output gaps tend to two.
questions.answer: Bounded domains give a uniform factor bound; the whole line does not.

questions.problem: A continuous function on a compact interval attains extrema and intermediate values. Which hypotheses serve each conclusion?
solution: Compactness and continuity give extrema.
Interval connectedness and continuity give intermediate values.

questions.problem: Prove zero derivative on an interval implies a constant function, and explain the disconnected-domain exception.
questions.hint: Apply the mean value theorem between arbitrary inputs.
solution: Their output difference is a derivative times the input difference, hence zero.
Two separated intervals can carry different constants while every derivative stays zero.
questions.answer: The conclusion holds on each interval component.

questions.problem: For $f(0)=0$, $f(x)=x^2\sin(1/x)$ when $x\ne0$, prove differentiability at zero and discontinuity of its derivative there.
questions.hint: Compare the difference quotient with the nonzero-point derivative.
solution: $f(h)/h=h\sin(1/h)\to0$.
Away from zero, the derivative $2x\sin(1/x)-\cos(1/x)$ keeps oscillating.
questions.answer: Differentiability does not guarantee derivative continuity.

questions.problem: Prove that changing finitely many values of a Riemann-integrable function to finite values preserves integrability and the integral.
questions.hint: Enclose exceptional points in intervals of arbitrarily small total width.
solution: Outside those intervals, sums agree or are controlled by the original integrability.
Extra uncertainty is at most a uniform height bound times their total length, hence can be arbitrarily small.
questions.answer: The new function is integrable with the same integral.

questions.problem: Why is derivative existence everywhere insufficient for this book's endpoint integral formula?
solution: A derivative need not be bounded or Riemann integrable.
The formula's derivative-integrability hypothesis cannot be omitted.
questions.answer: The required integrability must also hold.

reviews.title: Function sequences and limit interchange · Chapter review

questions.problem: Prove $x^n$ tends uniformly to zero on $[0,r]$ for fixed $0<r<1$, but not on $[0,1)$.
solution: The first domain has supremum error $r^n\to0$.
The second has supremum one at every index, or moving points with error one half.
questions.answer: Domain boundaries change uniform error control.

questions.problem: Why does uniform function convergence to zero not suffice for interchanging derivatives?
solution: $\sin(nx)/n$ has magnitude at most the reciprocal index.
Its derivative at zero stays one; the limiting zero function has derivative zero.
questions.answer: Function-amplitude control does not control derivatives.

exam.problem: In the square-root construction, how does a supremum whose square is too small lead to a contradiction?
exam.hint: Choose a sufficiently small positive increment.
solution: Keep $h(2s+h)<a-s^2$ so the new square remains below the target.
The new number exceeds the supremum yet belongs to the candidate set, a contradiction.
exam.answer: This rules out being too small; a smaller upper bound similarly rules out being too large.

exam.problem: A bounded real sequence has the same limit for every convergent subsequence. Prove the whole sequence converges.
exam.hint: Assume infinitely many terms lie outside one fixed error band.
solution: The bad subsequence is bounded and has a convergent subsequence.
Its limit stays outside the band, contradicting uniqueness of the subsequential limit.
exam.answer: Boundedness is essential to the argument.

exam.problem: Prove harmonic divergence with doubling blocks, then explain why vanishing adjacent differences do not suffice.
exam.hint: Compare partial sums at doubled indices.
solution: Each block contributes at least one half.
Adjacent reciprocal differences vanish, but distant tail partial sums remain separated.
exam.answer: The partial sums are not Cauchy.

exam.problem: Give a compact disconnected set and a connected noncompact set.
exam.hint: Use a finite set and an unbounded interval.
solution: Two distinct points form a compact disconnected set.
The real line is connected but unbounded, hence noncompact.

exam.problem: A real-line function has a uniformly bounded derivative magnitude. Prove uniform continuity.
solution: For a positive bound, take radius equal to error divided by the bound. For zero bound, the function is constant.

exam.problem: For squaring on zero to one with equal subdivisions, write both sums and find the integral.
solution: Both tend to one third.

exam.problem: Construct continuous functions tending pointwise to zero with every integral one.
solution: For indices at least two, use support $[0,2/n]$, center $1/n$, and height $n$.
Every fixed positive point eventually lies outside the support, and zero always has value zero; each triangular area is one.
exam.answer: Pointwise convergence does not suffice for integral interchange.

exam.problem: Explain why uniformly convergent derivatives still need convergent function values at one point, giving a counterexample without that condition.
solution: Constant functions $f_n(x)=n$ have identically zero, uniformly convergent derivatives.
The functions diverge everywhere, failing the anchor condition.

glossary.meaning: Real numbers support arithmetic and comparison, but division, roots, and reciprocals have conditions.
A supremum is the least upper bound; it need not belong to the set.
Natural numbers exceed every real bound; every nonempty open interval contains a rational.
Absolute value expresses distance in a form that can be bounded by adding errors.
A square root exists because a supremum fills the gap, not because curves seem to intersect.
Convergence requires every term after some cutoff to meet any prescribed positive error.
Control individual errors before combining them. Reciprocals require denominators bounded away from zero.
A bounded monotone real sequence converges to its appropriate supremum or infimum.
Every bounded real sequence has at least one convergent subsequence.
Closeness between tail terms tests convergence without knowing the limit beforehand.

glossary.term: A series is a limit of partial sums
glossary.meaning: An infinite series converges when its finite partial sums approach a finite real number.
Nonnegative terms make partial sums increasing. Convergence is then equivalent to boundedness above.
An eventual bound by a convergent geometric series establishes absolute convergence.
When magnitudes decrease to zero, alternating cancellation bounds the remainder by the next term.
Absolute convergence preserves the sum under rearrangement. Conditional convergence does not grant that freedom.

glossary.term: Open sets, closed sets, and relative topology
glossary.meaning: Every point of an open set has a neighborhood inside it. A closed set contains all its limit points.

glossary.term: Limit points, closure, and sequential criteria
glossary.meaning: The closure contains every point whose arbitrarily small neighborhoods meet the original set.
On the real line, compact means closed and bounded. Every open cover can then be reduced to finitely many members.
A real subset is connected exactly when it omits no point between two of its members.
Countable means listable by natural-number indices, not sparsely distributed.
A function limit controls nearby inputs. Continuity additionally makes that limit equal the value at the center.
A real function has a limit only if every admissible input sequence approaching the center gives the same output limit.

glossary.term: Continuous functions on compact sets and extrema
glossary.meaning: Continuous functions map compact sets to compact sets, ensuring both extrema are attained.
A continuous function cannot pass between two values while skipping a value between them.
Uniform continuity uses one input radius across the entire domain, independently of the center.
Differentiability writes the change as a linear main term plus a remainder smaller than the input change.

glossary.term: Rolle's theorem and the mean value theorem
glossary.meaning: Continuity on a closed interval and differentiability inside connect the average change to a derivative somewhere.

glossary.term: Derivatives may be discontinuous but cannot skip values
glossary.meaning: A derivative may oscillate discontinuously while still having the intermediate value property.
A Taylor polynomial approximates a function only when its remainder is genuinely small.
A convex graph lies below its chords and, when differentiable, above every tangent.

glossary.term: Partitions, upper sums, and lower sums
glossary.meaning: Bound the function throughout each subinterval, then add the bounding rectangle areas.
Integrability requires a partition with upper–lower gap below every prescribed positive error.

glossary.term: Integrability of continuous, monotone, and finite-jump functions
glossary.meaning: Continuous and monotone functions on closed bounded intervals are integrable, for different reasons.

glossary.term: The derivative of an accumulation integral
glossary.meaning: At a continuity point of the integrand, local averages approach its value, giving the accumulation function that derivative.

glossary.term: Integral evaluation, substitution, and integration by parts
glossary.meaning: An antiderivative's endpoint difference computes an integral only when the antiderivative and integrability hypotheses hold.
Pointwise convergence allows different waiting times for each input; uniform convergence uses one cutoff for the whole domain.

glossary.term: Uniform Cauchy convergence and the Weierstrass test
glossary.meaning: Control function differences by one uniform tail budget to prove uniform convergence of a sequence or function series.

glossary.term: A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous
glossary.meaning: Split the error into three parts, transferring change in the limit to one continuous approximating function.

glossary.term: Conditions for interchanging integrals and derivatives
glossary.meaning: Uniform convergence passes integrals on finite intervals, but alone does not pass derivatives.

glossary.term: Power series, convergence radii, and termwise operations
glossary.meaning: On smaller closed intervals inside the convergence radius, both the power series and its derivative series have uniform bounds.

appendices.title: Limsup, liminf, and the root test
appendices.text: For a bounded sequence, tail suprema form a nonincreasing sequence whose limit is the limsup; tail infima similarly define liminf. A limsup strictly below a number means every sufficiently late term is below it; a limsup strictly above a number means infinitely many terms exceed it. Apply these facts to index-th roots of absolute terms for the root test. Unbounded cases permit extended real values.

appendices.title: Compactness, closed boundedness, and sequential compactness
appendices.text: For boundedness, cover a compact set with integer-radius intervals and choose a finite subcover. For closedness, take an outside point and neighborhoods around each member of radius one third their distance apart. A finite subcover and the minimum of its radii give a neighborhood of the outside point avoiding the set. Closed bounded sets lie in a closed interval, whose compactness follows by bisection; a closed subset inherits compactness by adding its open complement to a cover. Bolzano–Weierstrass and closedness give convergent subsequences with limits in the set. Conversely, unboundedness supplies a sequence with growing magnitude, and nonclosedness one approaching a missing closure point; both violate that subsequence property.
appendices.latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R:\quad\text{compact}\iff\text{closed and bounded}\iff\text{every sequence has a convergent subsequence with limit in }K

appendices.title: Integral linearity, additivity, and tagged sums
appendices.text: A common refinement lets two functions use one partition. The triangle bound on oscillation proves integrability of linear combinations; taking limits of common tagged sums gives linearity. Splitting the interval and joining partitions proves interval additivity. A function bounded in magnitude by a constant has every tagged sum, and hence integral, bounded by that constant times the width. The Darboux criterion is equivalent to all sufficiently fine tagged sums being close to the integral: fix a small-gap partition, then an arbitrary fine mesh needs extra error only in pieces crossing its finitely many partition points. Their total width vanishes with the mesh; remaining pieces are controlled by the original sums.

appendices.title: Finite exceptions versus dense discontinuity
appendices.text: Finitely many exceptional points fit in intervals of arbitrarily small total length. Boundedness then makes their upper–lower contribution arbitrarily small. In contrast, the rational-indicator function has oscillation one on every positive-length interval, so every partition gap equals the full interval length. Finite sampling cannot establish density; exact bounds follow from proofs that rationals and irrationals are both dense.

appendices.title: Smooth does not mean analytic: a flat function
appendices.text: Set the value at zero to zero and elsewhere use the exponential of negative reciprocal square. Every nonzero-point derivative is a polynomial in the reciprocal times that exponential. With reciprocal square as a new variable, positive-term lower bounds for the exponential series show exponential growth dominates every fixed power. Thus all those polynomial-times-decay expressions vanish. Induction on difference quotients gives every derivative at zero as zero, continuously. Yet values at nonzero inputs are positive, so the zero Taylor series does not equal the function.

appendices.title: Differentiability of a one-variable inverse
appendices.text: Suppose a function is continuously differentiable near a point with nonzero derivative. Derivative continuity preserves its sign in a smaller neighborhood, and the mean value theorem gives strict monotonicity. A continuous inverse exists on the image interval. Its difference quotient is the reciprocal of the corresponding original quotient, whose limit is nonzero, so the reciprocal limit applies. Keep the branch restriction and do not apply the result at a zero derivative.

appendices.title: Improper integrals and numerical series
appendices.text: Define an integral on an infinite interval as a limit of finite-endpoint integrals, not by treating infinity as an ordinary endpoint. For a nonnegative nonincreasing function, integrals on unit intervals lie between neighboring integer-point values. Summing proves the integral test under those hypotheses. The finite-interval uniform convergence theorem cannot transfer unconditionally to infinite intervals: its total-length error bound fails.

appendices.title: Proof dependencies and later analysis
appendices.text: This book starts from the real complete ordered field. Exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions use familiar single-variable-calculus definitions and properties. A construction of logarithms by integration, then exponentials by inversion, belongs after the fundamental theorem and one-variable inverse theorem. General metric spaces, measure, Lebesgue integration, functional analysis, and multivariable real analysis are later independent courses. Finite diagrams and automatic tests do not replace general proofs.

body.title: Derive consequences of axioms
body.text: This book starts with the reals as a complete ordered field, rather than constructing them from decimals. Field axioms supply associative, commutative, and distributive laws, and inverses for nonzero elements.

body.title: Handle inequalities
body.text: Adding the same number preserves order. Multiplying by a positive number preserves it; multiplying by a negative number reverses it. Considering signs proves squares nonnegative.

body.title: Distinguish number systems
body.text: The rationals also form an ordered field, but some bounded-above subsets lack a least upper bound there. Completeness is the extra property needed for later limit theorems.

formalDefinition.text: In an ordered field, addition and multiplication of positive elements are compatible with order.
conditions: Division is defined only for nonzero divisors.
The real order is total and compatible with addition and multiplication.

derivation.text: Negative one is nonzero and its square is one.
Express the difference of two ordered numbers as a positive number.
Positive multiplication keeps that difference positive; negative multiplication makes it negative.

workedExamples.title: Multiplication by a negative number
workedExamples.problem: Solve: negative two times a real number is less than six.
steps: For $-2x<6$, division by negative two reverses the inequality.
$x>-3$; zero verifies the direction.

workedExamples.title: Order of reciprocals
workedExamples.problem: Compare reciprocals when $0<a<b$.
steps: Since $ab>0$, divide $a<b$ by $ab$.
This gives $1/b<1/a$.

practice.problem: Does $x^2<0$ have a real solution?
practice.hint: Consider positive, negative, and zero inputs.
solution: Every real square is nonnegative.

practice.problem: May an inequality be multiplied by a number of unknown sign without changing its direction?
practice.hint: Its sign must be known.
solution: Positive, negative, and zero multipliers have different effects.

practice.problem: Are the rationals missing a division rule?
practice.hint: A nonzero rational has a rational reciprocal.
solution: They lack completeness, not field operations.

practice.problem: Prove that $0<a<b$ implies $1/b<1/a$.
practice.hint: Check the sign of the denominator product first.
solution: $ab>0$, so multiplication by positive $1/(ab)$ preserves the inequality.
From $a<b$, obtain $a/(ab)<b/(ab)$.
Cancel to get $1/b<1/a$. Without first checking positivity, this step is not justified.
practice.answer: Cancel to get $1/b<1/a$. Without first checking positivity, this step is not justified.

lessons.title: Upper bounds, suprema, and completeness
lessons.subtitle: A supremum is the least upper bound; it need not belong to the set.
lessons.concept: A supremum is the least upper bound; it need not belong to the set.
lessons.intuition: Keeping every point to the left of a boundary is not enough. No smaller boundary may still bound the set.
objectives: Distinguish a maximum from a supremum

body.title: Distinguish a maximum from a supremum
body.text: A maximum belongs to the set and is at least every member. A supremum is the least of all upper bounds. An open interval may have a supremum without a maximum.

body.title: Use the approximation property
body.text: Within every positive distance below a supremum lies a set member. Otherwise a smaller number would be an upper bound.

body.title: State completeness
body.text: Every nonempty bounded-above real subset has a real supremum. Neither hypothesis may be dropped: the empty set has no least real upper bound.

formalDefinition.text: This book takes the least-upper-bound property as the completeness axiom.
formalDefinition.latex: s=\sup A\iff\bigl[\forall a\in A:a\le s\bigr]\land\bigl[\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists a\in A:s-\varepsilon<a\bigr]
conditions: The set is nonempty and bounded above in the reals.

derivation.text: A least upper bound is an upper bound.
Suppose some left neighborhood of the supremum contains no set member.
That gives a smaller upper bound, a contradiction.
Conversely, if a smaller number were an upper bound, use their difference as the error to find a member above it.

workedExamples.title: Open and half-closed intervals
workedExamples.problem: Find the supremum and maximum of $(0,1)$ and $(0,1]$.
steps: Both sets are bounded by one and approach it arbitrarily closely.
Only the second contains one.
workedExamples.answer: Both have supremum one; only the second has a maximum.

workedExamples.title: A discrete approach
workedExamples.problem: Find the supremum of $A=\{1-1/n:n\ge1\}$.
steps: Every term is less than one.
For a positive error, choose $n>1/\varepsilon$ to enter the left neighborhood of one.

practice.problem: Does an unbounded-above set have a real supremum?
practice.hint: A real supremum must first be an upper bound.
solution: Without a real upper bound there is no real supremum.

practice.problem: Must a supremum belong to its set?
practice.hint: Use an open interval.
solution: Its right endpoint is absent.

practice.problem: What is the supremum of $\{2,5,7\}$?
practice.hint: Find the finite set's maximum.
solution: Seven belongs to the set and is its least upper bound.

practice.problem: A nonempty bounded set $A$ has supremum $s$. Prove there are $a_n\in A$ with $a_n\to s$.
practice.hint: Apply the supremum approximation property at reciprocal errors.
solution: For every $n\ge1$, choose a member with $s-1/n<a_n\le s$.
Then $0\le s-a_n<1/n$.
Given $\varepsilon>0$, take $N>1/\varepsilon$. All $n\ge N$ satisfy $|a_n-s|<\varepsilon$.

learningCheck.question: What distinguishes a supremum from a maximum?
choices: Whether it is the greatest upper bound
Whether it must belong to the set

body.title: Rule out infinitely large reals
body.text: If the natural numbers had a real upper bound, take their supremum. A natural number close enough to it has a successor above it, a contradiction.

body.title: Find a rational
body.text: Between strictly ordered reals, choose a denominator making the scaled gap exceed one. The integer-part function then supplies an integer numerator strictly inside.

body.title: Distinguish density and completeness
body.text: Rationals occur in every interval but do not fill the real line. Density gives local approximation, not closure under every limit.

formalDefinition.text: The natural numbers are unbounded in the reals, and the rationals are dense there.
formalDefinition.latex: a<b\implies\exists m\in\mathbb Z,n\in\mathbb N:\ a<\frac mn<b
conditions: The denominator is a positive integer and the interval has strictly positive length.

derivation.text: Assume the natural numbers have a supremum.
Use approximation to choose a natural number close to it.
Its successor exceeds the upper bound.

workedExamples.title: Between two numbers
workedExamples.problem: Find a rational strictly between $1.41$ and $1.42$.

Numerator one thousand four hundred fifteen lies strictly inside the scaled interval.

workedExamples.title: Irrationals too
workedExamples.problem: Does every nonempty open interval contain an irrational?
steps: Choose a rational $r$ in the interval's interior.
Choose a sufficiently large positive integer $n$ so that $r+\sqrt2/n$ remains inside.
A rational plus a nonzero irrational is irrational.
workedExamples.answer: Yes. Existence of the square root of two is proved later.

lessons.title: Compactness and Heine–Borel
lessons.subtitle: On the real line, compact means closed and bounded. Every open cover can then be reduced to finitely many members.
lessons.concept: On the real line, compact means closed and bounded. Every open cover can then be reduced to finitely many members.
lessons.intuition: Closedness prevents missing boundary limits; boundedness prevents escape to infinity.

body.title: Define finite subcovers
body.text: An open cover covers every point at least once. Compactness requires a finite subfamily still covering the set, for every possible open cover.

body.title: Compactness implies closed and bounded
body.text: Integer-radius intervals cover the line; a finite subcover forces boundedness. For a point outside the set, neighborhoods based on distances to members, reduced to finitely many, leave a safe neighborhood around that outside point. Thus the set is closed.

body.title: Prove closed intervals compact
body.text: If an interval's open cover has no finite subcover, bisect and retain a half still lacking one. Nested shrinking intervals give a common point. An open set containing it eventually covers the whole retained interval, a contradiction. Closed subsets inherit compactness.

formalDefinition.text: Heine–Borel here uses the usual topology on the real line.
formalDefinition.latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R\text{ compact}\iff K\text{ closed and bounded}
conditions: Closed and bounded need not mean compact in an arbitrary metric space.

derivation.text: Assume an open cover of a closed interval has no finite subcover, then bisect repeatedly.
Its common point belongs to a covering open set, hence has a positive-radius neighborhood there.
A sufficiently small retained interval lies wholly in that open set, a finite subcover and a contradiction.

workedExamples.title: An open interval is not compact
workedExamples.problem: Exhibit an open cover proving $K=(0,1)$ noncompact.
steps: The sets $(1/n,1)$ for $n\ge2$ cover it.
Any finite subfamily has a positive smallest left endpoint and misses points nearer zero.

workedExamples.title: Finite sets
workedExamples.problem: Why is a finite real set compact?
steps: Choose one covering open set for each point.
Finitely many points require only finitely many chosen sets.

practice.problem: Is a closed bounded interval compact?

practice.problem: Does compactness require every given cover to be finite?

solution: Only a finite subcover must exist.

practice.problem: Prove a compact real set $K$ is bounded.
practice.hint: Use a specific countable open cover.
solution: Intervals $(-n,n)$, $n\ge1$, cover the real line and hence $K$.
Compactness gives a finite subcover. Let $M$ be the largest selected radius.
Its union lies in $(-M,M)$, so $K\subseteq(-M,M)$. The empty set is bounded too.
practice.answer: Its union lies in $(-M,M)$, so $K\subseteq(-M,M)$. The empty set is bounded too.

lessons.subtitle: A real subset is connected exactly when it omits no point between two of its members.

body.title: Define a separation
body.text: A separation divides a set into two nonempty, disjoint, relatively open parts. Relative openness, rather than openness in the whole line, is essential.

body.title: Connected sets cannot skip points
body.text: A missing point between two members separates the set using intersections with the open half-lines on either side.

body.title: Intervals admit no separation
body.text: Suppose an interval is separated. Choose one point in each part and take the supremum of one side between them. Relative openness of either part leads to a contradiction whichever part contains the boundary.

formalDefinition.text: The empty set and singletons are connected by convention.
formalDefinition.latex: A\subseteq\mathbb R\text{ connected}\iff x<z<y,\ x,y\in A\implies z\in A
conditions: Intervals may be open, closed, half-open, or unbounded.

derivation.text: A missing middle point gives separation by open half-lines.
For a supposed interval separation, take a boundary supremum between two selected members.
Whichever relatively open part contains the boundary either permits extending it or excludes the required approach, a contradiction.

body.title: Enumerate rationals
body.text: Arrange integer numerators and positive integer denominators in finite layers by size. Skip repeated fractions to list every rational.

body.title: Use a diagonal argument
body.text: Given any list of infinite binary sequences, construct a new sequence whose index-th bit differs from the index-th listed sequence's bit there. It differs from every row somewhere and is absent from the list.

body.title: Transfer to real numbers
body.text: Map binary bits to ternary zeroes and twos to inject into a real interval. The first differing digit outweighs every possible later cancellation, avoiding representation ambiguity. Thus the interval is uncountable.

formalDefinition.text: Countable means finite or in bijection with the naturals. The set of infinite binary sequences is uncountable.
conditions: The diagonal argument refutes any purported complete infinite list.
A finite display is not an infinite proof.

derivation.text: Assume a list contains every infinite binary sequence.
Flip each diagonal bit.
The new sequence differs from row number at that position, so the list is incomplete.

practice.problem: Prove $T(b)=\sum_{n\ge1}2b_n/3^n$ injects infinite zero–one sequences into $[0,1]$.
practice.hint: Find the first differing position of two sequences.
solution: Terms are nonnegative with total at most $\sum2/3^n=1$, so the map is defined and lands in $[0,1]$.
If the first difference is at $k$, its magnitude is $2/3^k$; later differences total at most $\sum_{n>k}2/3^n=1/3^k$.
Their images differ in magnitude by at least $1/3^k>0$. Combined with binary-sequence uncountability, this proves the interval uncountable.

lessons.concept: A function limit controls nearby inputs. Continuity additionally makes that limit equal the value at the center.

body.title: Specify the limit point and domain
body.text: Discuss a function limit at a limit point of its domain. Inputs must be in the domain and differ from the center. Relative endpoints use the available one-sided approach.

body.title: Separate limits from function values
body.text: Changing only the center value preserves a punctured limit but may break continuity. At an isolated domain point, every function is automatically continuous.

body.title: Work backward to a radius
body.text: For a square function at a fixed center, factor output error into input difference and a magnitude factor. First restrict the radius below one, then obtain a uniform estimate.

formalDefinition.text: Continuity at a domain point means outputs at all sufficiently nearby domain inputs approach the value there.
conditions: A function limit additionally requires the center to be a domain limit point and uses punctured neighborhoods.
For continuity, the center belongs to the domain.

derivation.text: First restrict inputs to within one of the center.
Factor the square error.
Choose a radius meeting both requirements.

practice.problem: Prove directly that $f(x)=x^2$ is continuous at every $a\in\mathbb R$.
practice.hint: Require the input error to be below both one and the needed proportional bound.
solution: Given $\varepsilon>0$, take $\delta=\min(1,\varepsilon/(2|a|+1))$.
If $|x-a|<\delta$, then $|x+a|\le|x-a|+2|a|<2|a|+1$.
Thus $|x^2-a^2|=|x-a||x+a|<\delta(2|a|+1)\le\varepsilon$.

body.title: Detect jumps
body.text: If two input sequences approach the same point but have different output limits, no common function limit exists. Continuity sequences may include the center; punctured-limit sequences must exclude it.

formalDefinition.text: The real sequential limit criterion quantifies over all admissible punctured input sequences.

conditions: The center is a limit point of the domain.

Inputs approach the center while outputs keep violating the bound.

body.title: Prove continuous images compact
body.text: Pull back an arbitrary open cover of the image under the continuous map. It gives a relatively open cover of the domain. Select finitely many by compactness, then map back.

body.title: Obtain bounds and extrema
body.text: A compact real image is closed and bounded. Approach its supremum by image members; closedness keeps that supremum in the image, giving a maximum. Similarly for a minimum.

body.title: Check missing hypotheses
body.text: The identity on an open interval is bounded but misses endpoint extrema. A discontinuous function on a closed bounded interval can be unbounded. The word “interval” alone is insufficient.

formalDefinition.text: A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact domain attains its maximum and minimum.
formalDefinition.latex: \exists x_m,x_M\in K:\ f(x_m)\le f(x)\le f(x_M)\quad\forall x\in K
conditions: The domain is nonempty and compact; the function is continuous and real-valued.

derivation.text: Take the image supremum and choose inputs whose values approach it.
Compactness gives a convergent input subsequence with limit still in the domain.
Continuity transfers the limit to the outputs.

practice.hint: Apply the maximum theorem to which function?
solution: If $f$ is continuous, so is $g=-f$.
The maximum theorem gives $x_*\in K$ with $-f(x)\le-f(x_*)$ for all $x\in K$.
Multiply by negative one to get $f(x_*)\le f(x)$, so $f$ attains its minimum at $x_*$.

body.title: Keep the interval and continuity hypotheses
body.text: The domain must contain the entire interval between the two inputs, with continuity throughout. A target between endpoint outputs is attained by an intermediate input.

body.title: Locate a boundary with a supremum
body.text: When the left value is below the target and the right above, take the supremum of inputs whose outputs are below it. Continuity rules out the boundary output being either too low or too high.

body.title: Separate existence from uniqueness
body.text: The theorem establishes existence only. Uniqueness needs extra information such as strict monotonicity. Bisection likewise does not show that all roots are unique.

formalDefinition.text: A continuous image of an interval is an interval.
conditions: The function is continuous on the closed interval; reversed endpoint-value order is handled similarly.

derivation.text: Take the supremum of inputs with output below the target.
If its output is too low, continuity permits moving farther right while remaining below.
If too high, continuity excludes arbitrarily close lower-output inputs on the left.
Both contradict the supremum, so the output equals the target.

workedExamples.problem: Does $f(x)=x^3-x-1$ have a root between one and two?
steps: The polynomial is continuous; endpoint values are negative one and five.
Zero lies between them, so the intermediate value theorem gives a root.
workedExamples.answer: Yes; this theorem alone does not give uniqueness.

practice.problem: Prove $x^3-x-1=0$ has exactly one root in $(1,2)$.
practice.hint: Prove existence and uniqueness separately.
solution: The polynomial is continuous, with $f(1)=-1$ and $f(2)=5$; the intermediate value theorem gives an interior root.
If $1\le u<v\le2$, then $f(v)-f(u)=(v-u)(v^2+uv+u^2-1)>0$.

workedExamples.problem: Continuous triangular spikes have center at the reciprocal index, support from zero to twice that reciprocal, and height one. How do they converge on zero to one?
steps: For each fixed positive input the spike eventually moves away; the value at zero is always zero.
The pointwise limit is continuously zero, but every supremum error is one.

practice.problem: Does pointwise convergence of continuous functions to a continuous function imply uniform convergence? Give a counterexample on $[0,1]$.
practice.hint: Use height-one triangular spikes moving toward zero.
solution: Let $f_n(x)=\max(0,1-|nx-1|)$ for $n\ge2$. Each function is continuous and zero at zero.
For fixed $x>0$, once $n>2/x$, $nx>2$ and all later values are zero. The pointwise limit is the continuous zero function.
But $f_n(1/n)=1$, so the supremum error remains one and convergence is not uniform.

body.title: Interchange integration and limits
body.text: If integrable approximations converge uniformly, first use small-gap partitions to prove the limit integrable. Then bound integral error by interval width times uniform function error.

body.title: Sufficient conditions for derivative interchange
body.text: If each function is continuously differentiable, derivatives converge uniformly to a continuous limit, and function values converge at one input, integral accumulation proves uniform convergence of the functions and differentiability of the limit.

body.title: Identify insufficient conditions
body.text: High-frequency sine divided by frequency tends uniformly to zero, but derivatives are high-frequency cosines. At zero, each derivative is one while the limiting function's derivative is zero.

formalDefinition.text: Integration and differentiation need different sufficient hypotheses.
conditions: Integration: a finite closed interval, each function Riemann integrable, and uniform convergence.
Differentiation: each function continuously differentiable, derivatives uniformly convergent, and function values convergent at one point.

derivation.text: Uniform error first establishes integrability of the limit, then controls integral differences.
For derivatives, write every function using its integral representation.
Uniform derivative error and the anchored value error together control the functions.
A continuous limit and the fundamental theorem identify the derivative.

workedExamples.title: Pointwise convergence is insufficient for integrals
workedExamples.problem: Triangular spikes have support zero to twice the reciprocal index, height equal to the index, and index at least two. What are their integrals?
steps: Every fixed input eventually lies outside the support, so values tend pointwise to zero.
Half the base times the height gives integral one for every spike.
workedExamples.answer: Integral limits are one, unlike the zero function's integral.

workedExamples.title: Uniform function convergence is insufficient for derivatives
workedExamples.problem: Let $f_n(x)=\sin(nx)/n$ converge uniformly on $[0,1]$. Each function is differentiable on the real line. Can derivatives at zero pass to the limit?
steps: Function magnitude is at most $1/n$, so convergence to zero is uniform.
$f_n'(0)=1$, but the zero function's derivative is zero.

practice.problem: Can uniformly convergent derivatives coexist with divergent functions if no value is anchored?

solution: All derivatives are zero, while each function may equal its index.

practice.problem: Construct continuous functions on $[0,1]$ tending pointwise to zero with every integral equal to one, and prove both facts.
practice.hint: Raise the moving triangular spike's height to its index.
solution: Let $f_n(x)=n\max(0,1-|nx-1|)$ for $n\ge2$. Its support is $[0,2/n]$ and peak at $1/n$.
At zero it vanishes; every fixed positive input is eventually outside the support, giving pointwise convergence to zero.
The triangle has base $2/n$ and height $n$, hence integral one. The zero limit has integral zero, so limit and integration cannot be exchanged here.

lessons.title: Power series, convergence radii, and termwise operations

lessons.concept: On smaller closed intervals inside the convergence radius, both the power series and its derivative series have uniform bounds.

objectives: Restrict to an interior closed interval

body.title: Define the radius
body.text: Take the limsup of index-th roots of coefficient magnitudes; its reciprocal is the radius, with extended zero and infinity conventions. Inside, convergence is absolute; outside, terms fail to tend to zero.

body.title: Restrict to an interior closed interval
body.text: Choose a slightly larger radius still inside convergence. Root or comparison estimates give geometric bounds. Extra index factors in derivative coefficients do not change exponential growth, so derivative series also have uniform control.

body.title: Differentiate and integrate termwise
body.text: Both function and derivative series converge uniformly on that closed interval, allowing the previous interchange theorems. Power-series coefficients are center derivatives divided by factorials. Conversely, an arbitrary smooth function still needs vanishing Taylor remainders to equal its series.

formalDefinition.text: Power series converge locally uniformly inside their radius and may be differentiated and integrated termwise there.
conditions: Use reciprocal zero equals infinity and reciprocal infinity equals zero.
Check convergence at boundary points separately.

derivation.text: Fix a closed-subinterval radius smaller than the convergence radius.
Control coefficients at a larger radius; the smaller radius absorbs derivative index factors.
Apply the M-test and limit-interchange theorem.

workedExamples.title: The geometric power series
workedExamples.problem: Find the radius and endpoint behavior of $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x^n$.
steps: All coefficients are one, giving radius one.
At the right endpoint all terms are one; at the left they alternate positive and negative one. Neither series converges.
workedExamples.answer: Its sum is $1/(1-x)$ on $(-1,1)$; both endpoints diverge.

workedExamples.title: Different endpoint behavior
workedExamples.problem: What happens at both endpoints for $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x^n/n$?
steps: The root test gives radius one.
The right endpoint is harmonic and divergent; the left is negative alternating harmonic and conditionally convergent.
workedExamples.answer: One radius does not imply equal endpoint behavior.

practice.problem: Does multiplying coefficients by the index change the derivative series' radius?

solution: The radius remains unchanged.

practice.problem: Find the radius and full real convergence interval of $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x^n/n$.
practice.hint: Use roots for the interior and check each endpoint.
solution: The coefficient root satisfies $n^{-1/n}\to1$, giving radius one. For $|x|<1$, convergence is absolute.
At $x=1$ the harmonic series diverges; at $x=-1$ the negative alternating harmonic series converges conditionally.
For $|x|>1$, terms fail to vanish, so the series diverges. The real convergence set is $[-1,1)$.
